title: Essentialism: what works, backed by research

scenes.text: Busy all day, and nothing that matters moved? The book Essentialism says: do fewer things, on purpose. Here's what actually works.

visual.headline: Do fewer things. Which tips really work?

scenes.text: Big idea one is a mindset. You always have a choice. Only a few things are truly vital. And every yes is a trade-off.

visual.headline: Only a few things are vital
visual.body: You always have a choice · every yes is a trade-off

scenes.text: Big idea two is a method. Explore what really matters. Eliminate the rest, with a graceful no. Then execute, until the essential becomes routine.
Its practical tools hold up. In one study, students expected to finish a thesis in about 34 days. They took 55. So build in a buffer.
But we found no study testing its 90 Percent Rule. Research shows if-then plans work: if a new request comes in, then ask what it replaces.
The book says play sharpens your thinking, but adult evidence is thin. What works: short breaks restore energy. After hard work, you may need more than ten minutes.
And small wins as the top motivator is a stretch. What works: track your progress, in writing. It raises your odds of reaching the goal.
The verdict: read it for the tools, especially if other people's requests run your calendar.

visual.headline: Read it for the tools
visual.body: Skip it if you already prioritize strictly

scenes.text: Sources for every claim are in the description.

audience: Busy professionals and managers deciding whether Essentialism is worth their time (YouTube, LinkedIn)
